**The Dance of Shadows and Light: A Meandering Reflection on Existence**

The world is a vast, humming machine of coincidences and contradictions, a place where the mundane and the sublime brush shoulders so casually that we often fail to notice. I’ve spent years—perhaps a lifetime—trying to make sense of the in-between spaces, the moments that exist just beyond the reach of language. This is my attempt to capture some of them, not because they demand resolution, but because they shimmer with the kind of quiet mystery that makes life feel worth living.

### **I. The Weight of Small Things**

There is a particular kind of magic in the ordinary. Not the grand, firework-burst of magic that announcing itself with fanfare, but the quiet, almost shy kind that hides in the folds of daily life. The way sunlight slants through a half-closed curtain in the late afternoon, turning dust motes into a constellation of fleeting stars. The scent of rain on hot pavement, that petrichor that carries with it the memory of a thousand childhood summers. The first sip of coffee in the morning, bitter and warm, grounding you in the present before the day’s noise can sweep you away.

We are taught to chase the extraordinary—careers, achievements, love that feels like a movie montage—but it’s the small things that anchor us. A handwritten note left on a pillow. The way a loved one hums absentmindedly while doing the dishes. The first crisp page of a new book, the anticipatory crack of its spine. These are the fragments that, when strung together, form the necklace of a life.

Yet, we so often overlook them. We are a species obsessed with bigness: bigger houses, bigger dreams, bigger tragedies. We measure our worth in the scale of ourambitions, forgetting that the weight of a life is not in its height but in its depth. A single, well-lived day can contain multitudes.

I remember a winter afternoon in my grandmother’s kitchen. She was making dumplings, her hands moving with the kind of practiced ease that comes from decades of repetition. The air was thick with the scent of ginger and garlic, the radio playing some old folk song in the background. I was eight, maybe nine, and my only job was to seal the edges of the dumplings with a fork, pressing the tines into the dough to create little ridges. It was tedious work, but I loved the ritual of it—the way the dough felt under my fingers, the way my grandmother would occasionally brush flour from my forehead with a flour-dusted thumb.

We didn’t talk much. Words weren’t necessary. The silence was comfortable, filled with the sounds of boiling water and the clatter of the fork against the wooden table. When the dumplings were finally done, we ate them with soy sauce and vinegar, the broth rich and steaming in the cold kitchen. That memory, more than any grand vacation or milestone birthday, feels like the essence of warmth to me. It was a moment of pure, unadulterated presence. No past, no future—just the dumplings, the steam, the love in the air like a visible thing.

Why do these moments resonate so deeply? Perhaps because they are untainted by the pressure of significance. They are not performances. They are not for an audience. They are simply *ours*, in the most intimate sense of the word.

### **II. The Myth of Permanence**

One of the most persistent illusions of human existence is the belief in permanence. We build cities, write laws, erect monuments, all in the hope that something—anything—will outlast us. But the truth is that everything is temporary. The grandest cathedrals will one day crumble. The most profound love will fade or change. Even the stars, those ancient beacons of the cosmos, are not eternal. They burn, they die, they collapse into black holes or scatter into dust.

This thought could be paralyzing. If nothing lasts, what is the point of anything? Why build, why create, why love?

And yet, we do. We build anyway. We love anyway. We create anyway.

Perhaps it is the impermanence that gives things their beauty. A sunset is breathtaking precisely because it is fleeting. A flower blooms for a day, maybe two, and then it withers—but in that brief span, it is perfect. The Japanese have a word for this: *mono no aware*, the pathos of things, the bittersweet awareness of impermanence. It is the feeling you get when you see cherry blossoms falling, or when you hold a child who is growing too fast, or when you realize that a chapter of your life is quietly closing.

I experienced this acutely a few years ago when I revisited the house I grew up in. The neighborhood had changed—trees that were once saplings now towered over the street, the playground where I spent countless afternoons had been replaced by a parking lot. The house itself was smaller than I remembered, the rooms a fraction of the size they had seemed in my childhood imagination. I stood on the sidewalk for a long time, staring at the front door, half-expecting to see my younger self come bounding out, backpack swinging, ready for school.

But of course, that version of me was gone. The house was just a house now, a vessel for new memories, new lives. It was a strange kind of grief—not for a person, but for a time, a version of the world that no longer existed except in the fading pages of my mind.

And yet, there was a strange comfort in it too. The impermanence meant that the past was not a prison. It was not a place I could return to, but it was also not a place I was bound to. I could carry the memories with me, like a collection of postcards from a country I had visited long ago, but I was free to keep moving forward.

### **III. The Stories We Tell Ourselves**

Humans are storytelling animals. We weave narratives around everything—our lives, our relationships, our failures, our triumphs. These stories give us a sense of coherence, a way to make sense of the chaos. But they are also, by nature, simplifications. They are the maps, not the territory.

I have a friend who, for years, told herself the story that she was "bad at relationships." Every failed romance, every misunderstanding, every moment of loneliness was evidence in support of this narrative. It became a self-fulfilling prophecy. She would enter new relationships with the quiet certainty that they would end, and so they did, because she was already emotionally checked out, waiting for the inevitable collapse.

One day, she met someone who refused to fit into the story. He was patient where she expected impatience, kind where she expected cruelty. At first, she waited for the catch, the moment when he would reveal himself to be just like all the others. But the moment never came. Slowly, painfully, she began to question the story she had been telling herself for so long. Maybe she wasn’t bad at relationships. Maybe she had just been bad at choosing the right people, or maybe she had been so afraid of failure that she had sabatoged herself before the failure could happen.

It took years of therapy and self-reflection, but she eventually rewrote her story. She is still her—flaws and all—but she no longer sees herself through the lens of inevitable failure. And as a result, her relationships changed. Not because she changed, exactly, but because the way she saw herself changed, and that altered how she engaged with the world.

This is the power of stories. They shape our reality. The stories we tell about our past define our present, and the stories we tell about our future shape our actions. But here’s the thing: we are the authors. We can revise, edit, even burn the old drafts and start again.

Of course, some stories are harder to shake than others. Trauma, for instance, has a way of embedding itself deep in the narrative, coloring every subsequent chapter. I know people who have spent their entire lives trying to outrun a single moment—a betrayal, a loss, a violence—that defined them in ways they never chose. The story becomes a cage, and the cage becomes a home, and the home becomes a prison.

But even then, there is hope. Stories can be rewritten. It is never too late to add a new chapter, to introduce a plot twist, to give the protagonist a different ending. It takes courage, and it takes time, and it often takes help from others who can hold the pen with us when our hands are too shaky to write. But it is possible.

I think of my own life, the stories I’ve told myself over the years. For a long time, I believed I was shy, that I was someone who stood at the edges of rooms, observing but never fully participating. And for a while, that was true. But then I started to notice the moments when it wasn’t true—the times I laughed too loudly in a restaurant, the times I spoke up in a meeting, the times I reached out to a stranger because something in their eyes made me think they needed a kind word. Slowly, I began to see that shyness was not an immutable part of my identity, but a role I had played for so long that I had forgotten it was just a role.

Now, I’m not sure if I’m shy or outgoing. Maybe I’m both. Maybe I’m neither. Maybe the question itself is less important than the realization that I don’t have to be any one thing. I can be a collection of contradictions, a work in progress, a story that is still being written.

### **IV. The Paradox of Connection**

We are born alone and we die alone, but in between, we spend our lives trying to bridge the chasm of that solitude. Connection is the great human project. We build families, friendships, communities, nations, all in the hope of touching and being touched, of knowing and being known.

And yet, true connection is elusive. Language, for all its power, is an imperfect tool. We use words to describe our inner worlds, but words are like nets—useful for catching fish, but not the ocean. There is always something that slips through. The depth of a feeling, the nuance of an experience, the inexplicable ache in the chest when you look at a certain photo or hear a certain song. We do our best to translate these things into sentences, but the translation is always a little off, like a poem that loses its rhythm when moved from one language to another.

This is why art exists. Music, painting, dance, literature—they are all attempts to communicate what cannot be communicated through ordinary means. A piece of music can convey grief in a way that words cannot. A painting can capture the essence of a mood that defies description. A dance can express joy or sorrow or longing with a single movement of the body.

But even art is limited. The artist can only express what they themselves understand, and the audience can only interpret it through the lens of their own experiences. What one person feels as profound, another might feel as empty. Connection, then, is not just about expression—it’s about reception. It’s about finding someone who, for a moment, tunes into the same frequency as you, who feels the same resonance in their bones.

I had a friend in college who understood me in a way that felt almost uncanny. We could sit in silence for hours, comfortable in the quiet, or we could talk for just as long about nothing and everything. There was no need to perform, no need to explain myself. He just *got* me. And I got him. It was the kind of friendship that feels like coming home.

Then, one day, he moved across the country. For a while, we stayed in touch—phone calls, texts, the occasional visit. But slowly, the distance took its toll. We drifted. Not because we wanted to, but because life has a way of pulling people in different directions. The last time we spoke, it was awkward. We struggled to find the easy rhythm that had once come so naturally. It was like trying to pick up a conversation in a language you hadn’t spoken in years. The words were there, but the music was gone.

I still think about him sometimes. I wonder if he still thinks about me. I wonder if, somewhere out there, there are other people who would *get* me in the same way he did. Maybe. Maybe not. But the fact that it happened once—that there was someone who saw me, truly saw me—makes me believe it can happen again.

Connection is not about permanence. It’s about moments. A shared laugh, a knowing look, a hand held in the dark. These are the threads that weave the tapestry of human experience, and even if the tapestry frays over time, the threads remain, testaments to the fact that, for a little while, we were not alone.

### **V. The Illusion of Control**

If there is one lesson life teaches us over and over again, it is that we are not in control. We plan, we strategize, we set goals, and then—inevitably—life throws us a curveball. A global pandemic. A sudden illness. A job loss. A betrayal. A natural disaster. These things remind us, in no uncertain terms, that the illusion of control is just that—an illusion.

And yet, we cling to it. We make to-do lists and five-year plans. We save money and buy insurance. We follow routines and rituals, all in the hope that we can impose some order on the chaos. There is a certain comfort in the illusion. It makes the world feel safer, more predictable. But when the illusion shatters—and it always does—we are left with the raw, terrifying truth: we are not the authors of our lives. We are, at best, co-authors, sharing the pen with fate, chance, and a thousand other forces we cannot see or understand.

I learned this lesson the hard way a few years ago. I had just been promoted at work, a position I had been working toward for years. I had bought a new car, moved into a nicer apartment, even started dating someone I genuinely cared about. Life, for the first time in a long time, felt like it was going *according to plan*. And then, in the span of a few weeks, everything fell apart. The relationship ended. I was diagnosed with a chronic illness. My mother, who had always been the rock of our family, suffered a stroke.

I remember sitting on the floor of my apartment one night, surrounded by the detritus of a life that was no longer mine—half-packed boxes, unopened mail, a half-empty bottle of wine—and feeling like I had been hit by a truck. The rug had been pulled out from under me, and I was free-falling through space with no idea when or where I would land.

For a while, I was angry. Angry at the universe, angry at myself, angry at the cruel joke of it all. I had done everything *right*. I had worked hard, played by the rules, been a good person. Why was this happening to me?

But anger, while cathartic, is not particularly productive. Eventually, I had to confront the truth: life does not owe us fairness. It does not owe us happiness. It does not owe us *anything*. The sooner we accept that, the sooner we can stop railing against the injustice and start figuring out how to live within it.

This is not to say that we should give up on planning or striving or hoping. There is value in setting goals and working toward them. But there is also value in holding those plans lightly, in recognizing that they are not guarantees, but rather best-case scenarios. The Stoics understood this well. They practiced *amor fati*—the love of fate—not in the sense of accepting everything that happens with passive resignation, but in the sense of embracing whatever comes, good or bad, as an opportunity to grow.

I’m not a Stoic. I still get frustrated when things don’t go my way. I still worry about the future. But I’m trying to cultivate a little more *amor fati* in my life. When my chronic illness flares up and I have to cancel plans, I try to remind myself that rest is also a form of productivity. When I face a setback at work, I try to ask: *What can I learn from this?* When I feel the old anger rising at the unfairness of it all, I try to breathe and remember that the universe is not *out to get me*. It is simply indifferent. And in that indifference, there is a strange kind of freedom.

If we are not in control, then we are also not responsible for everything that goes wrong. We can do our best, and then let go. We can love deeply, work hard, dream big—and then accept that the outcome is not entirely up to us. It is a humbling realization, but also, in its own way, a liberating one.

### **VI. The Beauty of Not Knowing**

We live in an age of information. The sum of human knowledge is quite literally at our fingertips, accessible with a few taps on a smartphone. We can learn how to bake a soufflé, speak Mandarin, or build a rocket ship with a quick Google search. And yet, for all our access to information, we are no closer to answering the big questions. What is the meaning of life? What happens after we die? Why are we here?

Some people find this lack of answers unsettling. They want certainty, a clear path, a rulebook to follow. But I have come to believe that not knowing is its own kind of beauty. The mystery is what makes life exciting. If we knew everything, if we understood every variable and could predict every outcome, existence would be a dull, predictable march toward a foreseeable end.

The not-knowing keeps us curious. It keeps us moving forward. It forces us to engage with the world, to ask questions, to seek, to wonder. It is the reason we create art, explore the cosmos, and fall in love. Because we don’t have all the answers, we are compelled to keep looking.

I think of the scientists who spend their lives studying the universe. They know more about the cosmos than any generation before them, and yet, the more they learn, the more they realize how much they *don’t* know. Dark matter, dark energy, the multiverse—these are not just gaps in our knowledge, but vast, yawning chasms. And yet, rather than being disheartened, most scientists I know are *thrilled* by this. The unknown is not a void to be feared, but a frontier to be explored.

The same is true of our inner lives. We are complex, contradictory creatures. We contain multitudes, as Whitman said. And yet, how little we truly understand about ourselves. Why do we fall in love with one person and not another? Why do certain memories haunt us while others fade into obscurity? Why do we sometimes act in ways that are completely at odds with our own values? The psyche is a labyrinth, and we are all Theseus, wandering the corridors, searching for the minotaur of self-knowledge.

But here’s the thing about labyrinths: the journey is as important as the destination. The not-knowing is not a problem to be solved, but a space to be inhabited. It is the difference between a life lived on autopilot and a life lived with wide-eyed wonder.

I have a friend who is a painter. She once told me that she never starts a painting with a clear vision of what it will look like. She begins with a color, a shape, a feeling, and then she lets the painting evolve organically. Sometimes it becomes something beautiful. Sometimes it doesn’t. But the process—the act of not knowing where she’s going, of trusting her instincts and the materials—is where the magic happens.

Life is like that. We can plan, we can prepare, we can have a general sense of direction. But the most meaningful moments often come when we surrender to the not-knowing, when we allow ourselves to be surprised, to be led by curiosity rather than certainty.

### **VII. The Art of Paying Attention**

The world is a noisy place. Between work and social media and the constant hum of modern life, it’s easy to go through the days in a fog, barely registering the world around us. We move from one task to the next, one distraction to the next, without ever really *seeing*.

But attention is a kind of love. When we pay attention—truly pay attention—to the people, places, and moments in our lives, we imbue them with significance. The poet Mary Oliver wrote, *"Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?"* The answer, I think, is to notice it. To be present for it. To not let the wild and precious slip through our fingers unnoticed.

I had a professor in college who taught a class on the art of observation. For one assignment, he had us sit in a park for an hour with a notebook, writing down everything we noticed. Not just the obvious things—the trees, the benches, the people—but the subtle details. The way the light filtered through the leaves. The sound of a child’s laughter echoing off the pavement. The scent of freshly cut grass. The way a pigeon hopped in a little circle before settling down to peck at a crumb. At first, it felt tedious. But after a while, something shifted. I began to see the park—not as a backdrop, but as a living, breathing entity, full of stories and secrets.

That exercise changed the way I move through the world. I started to notice more. The way my neighbor’s garden changes with the seasons. The way my cat’s ears twitch when she’s dreaming. The way the barista at my local coffee shop always has a different nail color. These are not earth-shattering observations, but they have enriched my life in ways I can’t quite explain. They have made me feel more *alive*.

Attention is also a way of honoring the people in our lives. Think about the last time someone truly listened to you—not just waiting for their turn to speak, but really *listening*, hanging on your words, asking questions, reflecting back what they heard. It’s a rare and powerful experience. It makes you feel seen, valued, understood.

We can offer that gift to others simply by paying attention. By putting down our phones during conversations. By asking follow-up questions. By remembering the little details—the name of someone’s child, their favorite book, the story they told about their grandmother’s cooking. These small acts of attention are the building blocks of connection.

But paying attention is not just about the external world. It’s also about the internal one. How often do we check in with ourselves, really listen to our own thoughts and feelings? We are so used to being *busy* that we forget to be *still*. We fill every moment with noise, afraid of what we might hear in the silence.

Meditation, journaling, even just a few minutes of quiet reflection each day—these are all ways of paying attention to ourselves. And what we often find when we do is that we are not who we thought we were. Our desires, our fears, our joys—they shift and change like the tides. Paying attention allows us to ride those tides rather than being drowned by them.

### **VIII. The Courage to Be Soft**

We live in a culture that often equates strength with hardness. We admire the stoic, the unshakable, the person who never cries, never falters, never shows weakness. We celebrate resilience, but we often confuse it with invulnerability. We are told to "toughen up," to "suck it up," to "get over it."

But there is another kind of strength—one that is softer, more pliable. The strength to be vulnerable. The strength to admit when we’re struggling. The strength to ask for help. The strength to feel deeply, even when it hurts.

The poet David Whyte writes, *"Vulnerability is not a weakness, a passing indisposition, or something we can arrange to do without, vulnerability is not a choice, vulnerability is the underlying, ever present and abiding under-current of our natural state."* To be human is to be vulnerable. It is to be open to joy and sorrow, to love and loss, to hope and despair. And yet, we spend so much energy trying to armor ourselves against these experiences, as if we could build a fortress high enough and strong enough to keep the world out.

But the world always finds a way in. And when it does, the armor often does more harm than good. It isolates us. It prevents us from connecting with others. It keeps us from fully experiencing the richness of life.

I have a friend who is one of the most emotionally open people I know. He cries at sad movies, gets tearful during heartfelt conversations, and isn’t afraid to say "I love you" or "I’m struggling." At first, I’ll admit, I found it a little disconcerting. I was raised in a household where emotions were not discussed, where strength meant keeping a stiff upper lip. But the more I’ve gotten to know my friend, the more I’ve come to admire his softness. It’s not a sign of weakness—it’s a sign of courage. The courage to be fully himself, to refuse to wear a mask, to let the world see him, scars and all.

There is a Japanese concept called *kintsugi*, the art of repairing broken pottery with gold. Instead of hiding the cracks, the artist highlights them, turning the damage into something beautiful. It is a metaphor for the way we might approach our own brokenness. We are all cracked in some way—by loss, by failure, by love, by life. But those cracks are not flaws to be hidden. They are proof of our resilience, of our ability to survive and even thrive despite the breaks.

Being soft does not mean being fragile. It means being *real*. It means allowing ourselves to feel the full spectrum of human emotion, from ecstasy to agony, without judgment or fear. It means recognizing that vulnerability is not the opposite of strength, but its foundation.

### **IX. The Longing for Home**

There is a kind of longing that resides deep in the human heart—a yearning for a place, a person, a feeling that we cannot quite name. The Germans call it *Sehnsucht*, a profound, aching desire for something unknown, something just out of reach. It is the feeling you get when you hear a piece of music that seems to echo a memory you’ve never had, or when you look at a landscape that feels familiar even though you’ve never been there.

This longing is often tied to the idea of home. But home, in this sense, is not just a physical place. It is a state of being, a sense of belonging, of safety, of wholeness. It is the place where we are fully known and fully loved. And yet, most of us spend our lives searching for it, chasing it, without ever quite finding it.

I felt this longing acutely when I was in my twenties, living in a new city, surrounded by new people, trying to build a new life. No matter how much I enjoyed my job, my friends, my hobbies, there was always a quiet ache in the background, a sense that something was missing. I would walk through the streets at night, looking up at the windows glowing with warm light, and feel a pang of envy for the people inside, laughing and talking and *belonging*.

It took me a long time to realize that the longing itself was not a sign that something was wrong with my life. It was simply a part of being human. The search for home is a universal experience. We are all, in some way, homeless, wanderers in a world that is both wondrous and strange.

But here’s the paradox: the more we chase home, the more elusive it becomes. Home is not a destination. It is a way of being. It is the ability to find comfort in the present moment, to feel at ease in our own skin, to recognize that we are already where we need to be.

I found a kind of home in my thirties, not in a place, but in a person. My partner has a way of making me feel seen and safe and understood in a way I never thought possible. But even that is not the whole story. Because ultimately, home is not something that can be found externally. It is something we carry within us. It is the quiet voice that says, *You are enough. You belong. You are where you need to be.*

This is not to say that the longing disappears. I still feel it sometimes—a twinge of nostalgia for a place I’ve never been, a person I’ve never met, a version of myself I’ve never quite become. But now, I see it not as a sign of lack, but as a sign of abundance. The longing is a reminder that I am alive, that I am capable of feeling deeply, that I am still searching, still growing, still becoming.

### **X. The Gift of Uncertainty**

I’ll end where I began: with the not-knowing. Because, in the end, that’s all we have. We don’t know where we’re going. We don’t know what’s around the next corner. We don’t know if our dreams will come true or if our fears will materialize. And that’s okay.

Uncertainty is not the enemy. It is the very fabric of life. It is what makes the journey exciting, what keeps us moving forward, what allows for the possibility of surprise, of growth, of transformation.

I have no grand conclusions to offer. No neatly tied-up answers. Only this: life is a dance of shadows and light, of joy and sorrow, of connection and solitude. It is messy and beautiful and fleeting. And the only way to live it fully is to show up, to pay attention, to love deeply, to feel bravely, and to keep dancing, even when we don’t know the steps.

So here’s to the not-knowing. Here’s to the in-between spaces. Here’s to the quiet moments and the loud ones, the tears and the laughter, the love and the loss. Here’s to the wild, precious, unpredictable gift of being alive.

But of course, that version of me was gone. The house was just a house now, a vessel for new memories, new lives. It was a strange kind of grief—not for a person, but for a time, a version of the world that no longer existed except in the fading pages of my mind.

And yet, there was a strange comfort in it too. The impermanence meant that the past was not a prison. It was not a place I could return to, but it was also not a place I was bound to. I could carry the memories with me, like a collection of postcards from a country I had visited long ago, but I was free to keep moving forward.

### **III. The Stories We Tell Ourselves**

Humans are storytelling animals. We weave narratives around everything—our lives, our relationships, our failures, our triumphs. These stories give us a sense of coherence, a way to make sense of the chaos. But they are also, by nature, simplifications. They are the maps, not the territory.

I have a friend who, for years, told herself the story that she was "bad at relationships." Every failed romance, every misunderstanding, every moment of loneliness was evidence in support of this narrative. It became a self-fulfilling prophecy. She would enter new relationships with the quiet certainty that they would end, and so they did, because she was already emotionally checked out, waiting for the inevitable collapse.

One day, she met someone who refused to fit into the story. He was patient where she expected impatience, kind where she expected cruelty. At first, she waited for the catch, the moment when he would reveal himself to be just like all the others. But the moment never came. Slowly, painfully, she began to question the story she had been telling herself for so long. Maybe she wasn’t bad at relationships. Maybe she had just been bad at choosing the right people, or maybe she had been so afraid of failure that she had sabatoged herself before the failure could happen.

It took years of therapy and self-reflection, but she eventually rewrote her story. She is still her—flaws and all—but she no longer sees herself through the lens of inevitable failure. And as a result, her relationships changed. Not because she changed, exactly, but because the way she saw herself changed, and that altered how she engaged with the world.

This is the power of stories. They shape our reality. The stories we tell about our past define our present, and the stories we tell about our future shape our actions. But here’s the thing: we are the authors. We can revise, edit, even burn the old drafts and start again.

Of course, some stories are harder to shake than others. Trauma, for instance, has a way of embedding itself deep in the narrative, coloring every subsequent chapter. I know people who have spent their entire lives trying to outrun a single moment—a betrayal, a loss, a violence—that defined them in ways they never chose. The story becomes a cage, and the cage becomes a home, and the home becomes a prison.

But even then, there is hope. Stories can be rewritten. It is never too late to add a new chapter, to introduce a plot twist, to give the protagonist a different ending. It takes courage, and it takes time, and it often takes help from others who can hold the pen with us when our hands are too shaky to write. But it is possible.

I think of my own life, the stories I’ve told myself over the years. For a long time, I believed I was shy, that I was someone who stood at the edges of rooms, observing but never fully participating. And for a while, that was true. But then I started to notice the moments when it wasn’t true—the times I laughed too loudly in a restaurant, the times I spoke up in a meeting, the times I reached out to a stranger because something in their eyes made me think they needed a kind word. Slowly, I began to see that shyness was not an immutable part of my identity, but a role I had played for so long that I had forgotten it was just a role.

Now, I’m not sure if I’m shy or outgoing. Maybe I’m both. Maybe I’m neither. Maybe the question itself is less important than the realization that I don’t have to be any one thing. I can be a collection of contradictions, a work in progress, a story that is still being written.

### **IV. The Paradox of Connection**

We are born alone and we die alone, but in between, we spend our lives trying to bridge the chasm of that solitude. Connection is the great human project. We build families, friendships, communities, nations, all in the hope of touching and being touched, of knowing and being known.

And yet, true connection is elusive. Language, for all its power, is an imperfect tool. We use words to describe our inner worlds, but words are like nets—useful for catching fish, but not the ocean. There is always something that slips through. The depth of a feeling, the nuance of an experience, the inexplicable ache in the chest when you look at a certain photo or hear a certain song. We do our best to translate these things into sentences, but the translation is always a little off, like a poem that loses its rhythm when moved from one language to another.

This is why art exists. Music, painting, dance, literature—they are all attempts to communicate what cannot be communicated through ordinary means. A piece of music can convey grief in a way that words cannot. A painting can capture the essence of a mood that defies description. A dance can express joy or sorrow or longing with a single movement of the body.

But even art is limited. The artist can only express what they themselves understand, and the audience can only interpret it through the lens of their own experiences. What one person feels as profound, another might feel as empty. Connection, then, is not just about expression—it’s about reception. It’s about finding someone who, for a moment, tunes into the same frequency as you, who feels the same resonance in their bones.

I had a friend in college who understood me in a way that felt almost uncanny. We could sit in silence for hours, comfortable in the quiet, or we could talk for just as long about nothing and everything. There was no need to perform, no need to explain myself. He just *got* me. And I got him. It was the kind of friendship that feels like coming home.

Then, one day, he moved across the country. For a while, we stayed in touch—phone calls, texts, the occasional visit. But slowly, the distance took its toll. We drifted. Not because we wanted to, but because life has a way of pulling people in different directions. The last time we spoke, it was awkward. We struggled to find the easy rhythm that had once come so naturally. It was like trying to pick up a conversation in a language you hadn’t spoken in years. The words were there, but the music was gone.

I still think about him sometimes. I wonder if he still thinks about me. I wonder if, somewhere out there, there are other people who would *get* me in the same way he did. Maybe. Maybe not. But the fact that it happened once—that there was someone who saw me, truly saw me—makes me believe it can happen again.

Connection is not about permanence. It’s about moments. A shared laugh, a knowing look, a hand held in the dark. These are the threads that weave the tapestry of human experience, and even if the tapestry frays over time, the threads remain, testaments to the fact that, for a little while, we were not alone.

### **V. The Illusion of Control**

If there is one lesson life teaches us over and over again, it is that we are not in control. We plan, we strategize, we set goals, and then—inevitably—life throws us a curveball. A global pandemic. A sudden illness. A job loss. A betrayal. A natural disaster. These things remind us, in no uncertain terms, that the illusion of control is just that—an illusion.

And yet, we cling to it. We make to-do lists and five-year plans. We save money and buy insurance. We follow routines and rituals, all in the hope that we can impose some order on the chaos. There is a certain comfort in the illusion. It makes the world feel safer, more predictable. But when the illusion shatters—and it always does—we are left with the raw, terrifying truth: we are not the authors of our lives. We are, at best, co-authors, sharing the pen with fate, chance, and a thousand other forces we cannot see or understand.

I learned this lesson the hard way a few years ago. I had just been promoted at work, a position I had been working toward for years. I had bought a new car, moved into a nicer apartment, even started dating someone I genuinely cared about. Life, for the first time in a long time, felt like it was going *according to plan*. And then, in the span of a few weeks, everything fell apart. The relationship ended. I was diagnosed with a chronic illness. My mother, who had always been the rock of our family, suffered a stroke.

I remember sitting on the floor of my apartment one night, surrounded by the detritus of a life that was no longer mine—half-packed boxes, unopened mail, a half-empty bottle of wine—and feeling like I had been hit by a truck. The rug had been pulled out from under me, and I was free-falling through space with no idea when or where I would land.

For a while, I was angry. Angry at the universe, angry at myself, angry at the cruel joke of it all. I had done everything *right*. I had worked hard, played by the rules, been a good person. Why was this happening to me?

But anger, while cathartic, is not particularly productive. Eventually, I had to confront the truth: life does not owe us fairness. It does not owe us happiness. It does not owe us *anything*. The sooner we accept that, the sooner we can stop railing against the injustice and start figuring out how to live within it.

This is not to say that we should give up on planning or striving or hoping. There is value in setting goals and working toward them. But there is also value in holding those plans lightly, in recognizing that they are not guarantees, but rather best-case scenarios. The Stoics understood this well. They practiced *amor fati*—the love of fate—not in the sense of accepting everything that happens with passive resignation, but in the sense of embracing whatever comes, good or bad, as an opportunity to grow.

I’m not a Stoic. I still get frustrated when things don’t go my way. I still worry about the future. But I’m trying to cultivate a little more *amor fati* in my life. When my chronic illness flares up and I have to cancel plans, I try to remind myself that rest is also a form of productivity. When I face a setback at work, I try to ask: *What can I learn from this?* When I feel the old anger rising at the unfairness of it all, I try to breathe and remember that the universe is not *out to get me*. It is simply indifferent. And in that indifference, there is a strange kind of freedom.

If we are not in control, then we are also not responsible for everything that goes wrong. We can do our best, and then let go. We can love deeply, work hard, dream big—and then accept that the outcome is not entirely up to us. It is a humbling realization, but also, in its own way, a liberating one.

### **VI. The Beauty of Not Knowing**

We live in an age of information. The sum of human knowledge is quite literally at our fingertips, accessible with a few taps on a smartphone. We can learn how to bake a soufflé, speak Mandarin, or build a rocket ship with a quick Google search. And yet, for all our access to information, we are no closer to answering the big questions. What is the meaning of life? What happens after we die? Why are we here?

Some people find this lack of answers unsettling. They want certainty, a clear path, a rulebook to follow. But I have come to believe that not knowing is its own kind of beauty. The mystery is what makes life exciting. If we knew everything, if we understood every variable and could predict every outcome, existence would be a dull, predictable march toward a foreseeable end.

The not-knowing keeps us curious. It keeps us moving forward. It forces us to engage with the world, to ask questions, to seek, to wonder. It is the reason we create art, explore the cosmos, and fall in love. Because we don’t have all the answers, we are compelled to keep looking.

I think of the scientists who spend their lives studying the universe. They know more about the cosmos than any generation before them, and yet, the more they learn, the more they realize how much they *don’t* know. Dark matter, dark energy, the multiverse—these are not just gaps in our knowledge, but vast, yawning chasms. And yet, rather than being disheartened, most scientists I know are *thrilled* by this. The unknown is not a void to be feared, but a frontier to be explored.

The same is true of our inner lives. We are complex, contradictory creatures. We contain multitudes, as Whitman said. And yet, how little we truly understand about ourselves. Why do we fall in love with one person and not another? Why do certain memories haunt us while others fade into obscurity? Why do we sometimes act in ways that are completely at odds with our own values? The psyche is a labyrinth, and we are all Theseus, wandering the corridors, searching for the minotaur of self-knowledge.

But here’s the thing about labyrinths: the journey is as important as the destination. The not-knowing is not a problem to be solved, but a space to be inhabited. It is the difference between a life lived on autopilot and a life lived with wide-eyed wonder.

I have a friend who is a painter. She once told me that she never starts a painting with a clear vision of what it will look like. She begins with a color, a shape, a feeling, and then she lets the painting evolve organically. Sometimes it becomes something beautiful. Sometimes it doesn’t. But the process—the act of not knowing where she’s going, of trusting her instincts and the materials—is where the magic happens.

Life is like that. We can plan, we can prepare, we can have a general sense of direction. But the most meaningful moments often come when we surrender to the not-knowing, when we allow ourselves to be surprised, to be led by curiosity rather than certainty.

### **VII. The Art of Paying Attention**

The world is a noisy place. Between work and social media and the constant hum of modern life, it’s easy to go through the days in a fog, barely registering the world around us. We move from one task to the next, one distraction to the next, without ever really *seeing*.

But attention is a kind of love. When we pay attention—truly pay attention—to the people, places, and moments in our lives, we imbue them with significance. The poet Mary Oliver wrote, *"Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?"* The answer, I think, is to notice it. To be present for it. To not let the wild and precious slip through our fingers unnoticed.

I had a professor in college who taught a class on the art of observation. For one assignment, he had us sit in a park for an hour with a notebook, writing down everything we noticed. Not just the obvious things—the trees, the benches, the people—but the subtle details. The way the light filtered through the leaves. The sound of a child’s laughter echoing off the pavement. The scent of freshly cut grass. The way a pigeon hopped in a little circle before settling down to peck at a crumb. At first, it felt tedious. But after a while, something shifted. I began to see the park—not as a backdrop, but as a living, breathing entity, full of stories and secrets.

That exercise changed the way I move through the world. I started to notice more. The way my neighbor’s garden changes with the seasons. The way my cat’s ears twitch when she’s dreaming. The way the barista at my local coffee shop always has a different nail color. These are not earth-shattering observations, but they have enriched my life in ways I can’t quite explain. They have made me feel more *alive*.

Attention is also a way of honoring the people in our lives. Think about the last time someone truly listened to you—not just waiting for their turn to speak, but really *listening*, hanging on your words, asking questions, reflecting back what they heard. It’s a rare and powerful experience. It makes you feel seen, valued, understood.

We can offer that gift to others simply by paying attention. By putting down our phones during conversations. By asking follow-up questions. By remembering the little details—the name of someone’s child, their favorite book, the story they told about their grandmother’s cooking. These small acts of attention are the building blocks of connection.

But paying attention is not just about the external world. It’s also about the internal one. How often do we check in with ourselves, really listen to our own thoughts and feelings? We are so used to being *busy* that we forget to be *still*. We fill every moment with noise, afraid of what we might hear in the silence.

Meditation, journaling, even just a few minutes of quiet reflection each day—these are all ways of paying attention to ourselves. And what we often find when we do is that we are not who we thought we were. Our desires, our fears, our joys—they shift and change like the tides. Paying attention allows us to ride those tides rather than being drowned by them.

### **VIII. The Courage to Be Soft**

We live in a culture that often equates strength with hardness. We admire the stoic, the unshakable, the person who never cries, never falters, never shows weakness. We celebrate resilience, but we often confuse it with invulnerability. We are told to "toughen up," to "suck it up," to "get over it."

But there is another kind of strength—one that is softer, more pliable. The strength to be vulnerable. The strength to admit when we’re struggling. The strength to ask for help. The strength to feel deeply, even when it hurts.

The poet David Whyte writes, *"Vulnerability is not a weakness, a passing indisposition, or something we can arrange to do without, vulnerability is not a choice, vulnerability is the underlying, ever present and abiding under-current of our natural state."* To be human is to be vulnerable. It is to be open to joy and sorrow, to love and loss, to hope and despair. And yet, we spend so much energy trying to armor ourselves against these experiences, as if we could build a fortress high enough and strong enough to keep the world out.

But the world always finds a way in. And when it does, the armor often does more harm than good. It isolates us. It prevents us from connecting with others. It keeps us from fully experiencing the richness of life.

I have a friend who is one of the most emotionally open people I know. He cries at sad movies, gets tearful during heartfelt conversations, and isn’t afraid to say "I love you" or "I’m struggling." At first, I’ll admit, I found it a little disconcerting. I was raised in a household where emotions were not discussed, where strength meant keeping a stiff upper lip. But the more I’ve gotten to know my friend, the more I’ve come to admire his softness. It’s not a sign of weakness—it’s a sign of courage. The courage to be fully himself, to refuse to wear a mask, to let the world see him, scars and all.

There is a Japanese concept called *kintsugi*, the art of repairing broken pottery with gold. Instead of hiding the cracks, the artist highlights them, turning the damage into something beautiful. It is a metaphor for the way we might approach our own brokenness. We are all cracked in some way—by loss, by failure, by love, by life. But those cracks are not flaws to be hidden. They are proof of our resilience, of our ability to survive and even thrive despite the breaks.

Being soft does not mean being fragile. It means being *real*. It means allowing ourselves to feel the full spectrum of human emotion, from ecstasy to agony, without judgment or fear. It means recognizing that vulnerability is not the opposite of strength, but its foundation.

### **IX. The Longing for Home**

There is a kind of longing that resides deep in the human heart—a yearning for a place, a person, a feeling that we cannot quite name. The Germans call it *Sehnsucht*, a profound, aching desire for something unknown, something just out of reach. It is the feeling you get when you hear a piece of music that seems to echo a memory you’ve never had, or when you look at a landscape that feels familiar even though you’ve never been there.

This longing is often tied to the idea of home. But home, in this sense, is not just a physical place. It is a state of being, a sense of belonging, of safety, of wholeness. It is the place where we are fully known and fully loved. And yet, most of us spend our lives searching for it, chasing it, without ever quite finding it.

I felt this longing acutely when I was in my twenties, living in a new city, surrounded by new people, trying to build a new life. No matter how much I enjoyed my job, my friends, my hobbies, there was always a quiet ache in the background, a sense that something was missing. I would walk through the streets at night, looking up at the windows glowing with warm light, and feel a pang of envy for the people inside, laughing and talking and *belonging*.

It took me a long time to realize that the longing itself was not a sign that something was wrong with my life. It was simply a part of being human. The search for home is a universal experience. We are all, in some way, homeless, wanderers in a world that is both wondrous and strange.

But here’s the paradox: the more we chase home, the more elusive it becomes. Home is not a destination. It is a way of being. It is the ability to find comfort in the present moment, to feel at ease in our own skin, to recognize that we are already where we need to be.

I found a kind of home in my thirties, not in a place, but in a person. My partner has a way of making me feel seen and safe and understood in a way I never thought possible. But even that is not the whole story. Because ultimately, home is not something that can be found externally. It is something we carry within us. It is the quiet voice that says, *You are enough. You belong. You are where you need to be.*

This is not to say that the longing disappears. I still feel it sometimes—a twinge of nostalgia for a place I’ve never been, a person I’ve never met, a version of myself I’ve never quite become. But now, I see it not as a sign of lack, but as a sign of abundance. The longing is a reminder that I am alive, that I am capable of feeling deeply, that I am still searching, still growing, still becoming.

### **X. The Gift of Uncertainty**

I’ll end where I began: with the not-knowing. Because, in the end, that’s all we have. We don’t know where we’re going. We don’t know what’s around the next corner. We don’t know if our dreams will come true or if our fears will materialize. And that’s okay.

Uncertainty is not the enemy. It is the very fabric of life. It is what makes the journey exciting, what keeps us moving forward, what allows for the possibility of surprise, of growth, of transformation.

I have no grand conclusions to offer. No neatly tied-up answers. Only this: life is a dance of shadows and light, of joy and sorrow, of connection and solitude. It is messy and beautiful and fleeting. And the only way to live it fully is to show up, to pay attention, to love deeply, to feel bravely, and to keep dancing, even when we don’t know the steps.

So here’s to the not-knowing. Here’s to the in-between spaces. Here’s to the quiet moments and the loud ones, the tears and the laughter, the love and the loss. Here’s to the wild, precious, unpredictable gift of being alive.
